citation: corpus/herdr-0.8.0/api-schema.json, which herdr generates from its own request types and ./dev checks the running daemon against. Method names and every parameter here are declared there: PaneSplitParams (cwd, direction, env, focus, ratio, target_pane_id, workspace_id), TabCreateParams (cwd, env, focus, label, workspace_id), WorkspaceCreateParams (cwd, env, focus, label), LayoutSetSplitRatioParams (pane_id, path, ratio, tab_id), PaneResizeParams (amount, direction, pane_id), PaneZoomParams (mode, pane_id) whose mode defaults to toggle. The direction pair, and the fact that herdr has only two of the four sides, are recorded in docs/observations/herdr-0.8.0.md section 14.
why:
herdr ignores a parameter it does not recognise rather than refusing the request (`observations/herdr-0.8.0.md` section 6), so a misspelled key does not fail - it acts on whatever the daemon happened to have focused. `pane.split` is the sharp one: it takes `target_pane_id` where every other pane verb takes `pane_id`, and sending the wrong one splits an arbitrary pane. Against a real daemon holding one workspace and one pane, that is indistinguishable from correct, which is why these are pinned by name here rather than left to the daemon-backed tests. The second half is the direction pair: Muster names a split for the arrangement it produces and herdr for where the new pane goes, and `layout.rs` reads that same pair back in reverse - so getting it wrong here makes a column that reads back as a row.

The third subject here is the environment a pane-creating call carries, and it is the one whose failure is silent in a new way. Muster points its daemon at a config file of its own with HERDR_CONFIG_PATH, and a pane's process inherits the daemon's environment - so without a restore, `herdr` run inside a Muster pane reads Muster's derived file rather than the person's own. Every case that makes a pane shows the restore, and every case that does not shows its absence, because a reviewer reading one case should not have to hold the other eight in their head. What the cases cannot say is that the set is complete; `every_pane_a_daemon_makes_is_handed_the_users_own_config` says that, by reading which methods herdr declares an `env` on.

The ratios and amounts here are `f32` on the wire, which is why this file declares `numbers`. Without it the only fractions a case could write were the ones binary spells exactly - halves, quarters, eighths - and herdr's own default resize step of 0.05 was unsayable, because the driver's answer comes back widened to 0.05000000074505806. The declaration makes both sides narrow before they are compared, so a case states the number a person would write and still fails on a wrong one.

cases.name: a split names the pane to split, in the key only pane.split uses
cases.why: The silent one. `pane_id` here is dropped without complaint and herdr splits whichever pane it has focused, which in a window with one pane looks exactly right. Also the absent half of the envelope: no ratio and no directory are asked for, because sending nulls would be Muster stating a preference it does not have. herdr's own default ratio is what a keybinding wants, and its default directory is the one the split came from - which is what somebody splitting a pane mid-task means.

cases.name: a row is a split downwards
cases.why: Muster names a split for the arrangement it makes and herdr for where the pane went. layout.rs reads the same pair backwards, so a wrong mapping here produces a tree that disagrees with itself.

cases.name: a dragged-out split states both
cases.why: The other half of the same rule: a drag has an opinion about the ratio, and a pane opened for a directory has one about where it starts.

cases.name: splitting leftward starts as a rightward split
cases.why: herdr's SplitDirection is right and down, and a split always puts the new pane on the second side, so a leftward split has no request behind it: it is this one followed by pane.swap of the pair. What is pinned here is the first half, which is the half that reaches the wire as a `pane.split` - identical to a rightward split, deliberately, because the side is not something herdr can be told. The pair is checked end to end against a real daemon in crates/muster-herdr/tests/split_sides.rs.

cases.name: splitting upward starts as a downward split
cases.why: The other half of the same pair, on the other axis.

cases.name: a ratio turns round when the pair will be swapped
cases.why: Muster's ratio is the share the pane being split keeps, on all four sides, so that one number means one thing. herdr's is the *first* child's share, and after the swap the pane being split is the second child - so the two count from opposite ends and the number has to be inverted on the way out. A keybinding never notices, because it sends no ratio and herdr's default is symmetric; a drag-to-split or a CLI placing a divider at a quarter would otherwise get three quarters.

cases.name: a tab names a workspace the intent never carried
cases.why:
`tab.create` takes a workspace and nothing else - there is no `pane_id` it would accept - and a hopeful one would be ignored, putting the tab wherever that daemon was focused.

The intent names the pane the tab goes beside and no workspace at all (MIP-2): a workspace is herdr's unit for a whole project, and the core stopped carrying one. Which workspace that pane is in is a question only the daemon can answer, so `HerdrBackend::workspace_for` asks it with `pane.get` before this is built, and the answer arrives here as `workspace`. That is one extra round trip on a request somebody makes a few times an hour, and it is what stops the tab landing in whichever workspace the daemon last had focused.

cases.name: a tab with nowhere named falls back to the daemon's own rule
cases.why: Reachable when the pane the tab goes beside has no directory yet. A home directory is a worse answer than the one somebody wanted, and a better one than refusing to make the tab. The workspace is still named, because it is not the caller's to leave out - see the case above.

cases.name: a workspace names nothing, and lets herdr label it
cases.why: The intent asked for when there is nothing: a daemon Muster just started holds no panes. A label invented here would be a second naming scheme for something herdr already names, and the null is explicit because the key exists and Muster is declining it.

cases.name: closing and focusing a pane use the ordinary key
cases.why: The counterweight to the split case: `pane_id` is right everywhere except pane.split, so a reader who learns target_pane_id from that one case would spread it.

cases.name: focus names the pane the daemon should call looked-at
cases.why: Written rather than read: Muster routes input by its own cursor and tells the daemon so that whatever it computes from focus has been told (architecture.md, cursors are written, not read).

cases.name: a dragged divider is addressed by the turns down to it
cases.why: Dividers have no ids - a divider is a position in a shape that changes under it - so the path is how herdr names one. First is false and second is true, which is the same spelling layout.rs reads trees back with.

cases.name: the root divider is an empty path, not a missing one
cases.why: Dragging the only divider in a tab takes no turns to reach. An omitted path is a different request - herdr requires one - so this pins that zero turns is spelled as an empty array.

cases.name: resizing names a pane and a direction, and no divider
cases.why: The difference from layout.set_split_ratio, which is the other way to move the same line. A chord means `this pane bigger`; which divider achieves that is a question about a tree the person pressing it is not looking at, and only the daemon holds the rectangles that answer it.

cases.name: an amount is sent only when somebody meant one
cases.why: A keybinding wants the daemon's own step, and stating a number here would be Muster inventing a step size it has no opinion about. A CLI or an agent placing a divider exactly says.

cases.name: a resize amount is a share of the region, never a count of cells
cases.why:
herdr adds `amount` straight to a split's ratio and clamps it to 0.5 (observations, section 19), so any number at or above one is the same maximal jump. Muster sent cells here for a release: every `resize_step` a person could write - `1c`, `1px`, `10c` - arrived at or above one and moved half the pane, which made the key look like it had a single behaviour rather than a broken unit. This case is the unit itself, so a step that ever arrives whole again fails here rather than in somebody's hands.

The number is herdr's own default step, which is the one a person is most likely to write and the one this file could not state until it declared its width.

cases.name: zoom asks for a toggle by not asking for anything
cases.why: herdr's own default for `mode` is toggle, which is what one key means. Sending it would be Muster restating a default it agrees with - and the day that default changes is the day this should notice rather than quietly keep the old behaviour.

cases.name: naming a pane sends the name under herdr's own key
cases.why:
The ordinary case. `label` is herdr's word for a name somebody gave a pane, and it sits beside the terminal title rather than replacing it - the daemon never writes one over the other, so a named pane still says what it is doing.

Emoji go through unchanged, which is worth a case rather than an assumption: this is a field a person types into and `🔥 payments spike` is the sort of thing they type.

cases.name: taking a pane's name away is a null, not an empty string
cases.why:
herdr's `label` on a pane is nullable, and null is its spelling for having no name - an empty string would be a name that renders as a blank row and cannot be told from an unnamed one.

Sending the key at all is the load-bearing part. Omitting it leaves the name alone, so a clear that sent nothing would look like it worked and change nothing.

cases.name: naming a tab uses the tab's own verb
cases.why: A tab and a pane are renamed by different requests, and the tab's is the one every client hears about: herdr emits `tab.renamed` with the new label and emits nothing at all for a pane (observations/herdr-0.8.0.md section 16).

cases.name: taking a tab's name away is an empty string, because herdr has no null for it
cases.why:
The asymmetry, and the reason these are two intents rather than one verb over a target. `tab.rename` declares `label` a required string where `pane.rename` declares it nullable, so a null is a schema violation and the empty string is all there is.

It does not do what it looks like it does, and that is recorded rather than papered over: herdr keeps the empty name instead of restoring the tab's position number, and the empty name survives a daemon restart. Muster's own caption reads an all-digits or empty label as unnamed and draws its own place, so the window is right and herdr's interface is left showing a blank tab. The upstream ask is for a nullable label here.

cases.name: a drag within one tab exchanges two panes
cases.why:
The same request the leftward-split rearrange has always sent, asked for on its own. An exchange rather than an insertion because a tree has no 'between': the only well-defined thing a drag can mean over an arrangement is that these two swap places.

Both ids are named, and `source_pane_id` is the one being dragged. herdr moves its own cursor to the source whatever was focused before, which is a fact about the daemon rather than about Muster - Muster's keyboard is its own and this does not touch it.

cases.name: a drag into another tab is a move, and lands behind the row it was dropped on
cases.why:
herdr refuses a swap across tabs (`cross_tab`), so the other half of the same gesture is a different verb. `destination` is a tagged object because `pane.move` can also make a tab or a workspace to move into; Muster only ever names an existing one, since a drop landed on a row in it.

`split: right` is how 'after' is spelled. herdr puts the moved pane on the `second` side and reads a split first-then-second, so rightward is exactly one place later in the order the agent list shows. Its `SplitDirection` has only `right` and `down`, which is why the intent says an ordering and this says a geometry.

`focus: false` because arranging the list is not going somewhere. A drag that took the keyboard would interrupt whatever was being typed into the pane that had it.

cases.name: a pane pulled into a tab of its own is one move, and names the tab
cases.why:
The other destination `pane.move` offers, and the reason this exists at all: making a tab and then moving into it starts a login shell nobody asked for - an ssh session too, on another machine - takes the keyboard into it, and leaves a stray tab behind if anything fails between the two requests.

`workspace_id` is deliberately absent. On `tab.create` omitting it drops the tab into whichever workspace the daemon last had focused, which is why that request names one; here herdr already has the pane and a pane names its workspace. Measured against a real daemon in `pane_arranging.rs`, with another workspace focused, and the tab lands beside the pane it came from.

`label` is what to call the new tab, which the three-command dance could not set at all: it made the tab before anything knew what was going into it.

`focus: false` on the same terms as the case above - pulling a pane out of a split is arranging the window rather than going somewhere.

cases.name: a tab of its own with no name carries no label at all
cases.why: Absent rather than empty, the same distinction `tab.rename` draws in the other direction: herdr labels an unnamed tab by its place in the workspace, and an empty string is a name somebody typed. Sending one would give the tab a name nobody chose and no way to tell it from one they did.

cases.name: closing a tab names the tab and nothing else
cases.why: `tab.close` takes herdr's `TabTarget`, which is a tab id and nothing more - so there is no `force`, no list of panes, and nothing to get wrong except the id. It is here anyway because the verb ends more than it names: one request closes every pane in the tab, which is why Muster sends it rather than closing them one at a time and being interrupted half way.

cases.name: a daemon Muster did not point anywhere is sent nothing to restore
cases.why: A daemon named by `socket` in the config file is somebody else's, and a daemon on another machine was reached rather than started - neither had its config redirected, so a pane on either already reads the file it always did. Sending a path anyway would be worse than useless on the remote one: it names a file on this machine, and the pane is on that one.

cases.name: a verb that makes no pane carries no environment even where one is known
cases.why: Closing a pane, focusing one, moving a divider: herdr declares no `env` on any of them, and it ignores a parameter it does not declare rather than refusing it. So a stray one costs nothing today and is a silent behaviour change the day that method grows one - which is the same shape of fault as the misspelled key this file exists for, arrived at from the other direction.

cases.name: somebody who names their own herdr config is handed that one back
cases.why: HERDR_CONFIG_PATH is herdr's own way of naming a config file, and a person who exported it in their shell profile means it. Restoring the XDG default instead would point their pane at a file they had already said they do not use - which is the whole fault this restore exists to prevent, reintroduced by the fix for it. Precedence follows herdr's own: the explicit path wins, and the config directory answers when nothing does.

cases.name: a read asks for as far back as herdr will go, whatever was wanted
cases.why:
Two choices in one request, and both are the whole of it.

The source: `recent` returns grid rows, so a match's place in the answer is already the offset to scroll to; `recent_unwrapped` returns whole logical lines and would leave every hit unlocatable. Both are valid values and herdr would accept either, so nothing but this pins which one a read is built on. A find and `muster pane read` are the same request - one matches the answer and one prints it - so the source has to be right for both.

The count: always herdr's maximum, never what the caller asked for. `recent` counts grid rows up from the bottom of the pane, and the bottom of an idle pane is the blank remainder of its viewport - so `lines: 12` on a pane sitting at a prompt buys twelve blank rows, which trim away to nothing and answer `""`. That is byte-identical to a pane that has printed nothing, and it is the pane you most often read to find out whether it is quiet. So `--rows` is counted after the answer arrives, where a row is a row of text (`PaneText::tail`). What it costs is the whole thousand on the wire per read, which is a person or an agent asking a question rather than anything on the render path.

`strip_ansi` is herdr's default, sent anyway because a default that moved would start handing back escape codes.

cases.name: a pane Muster named goes out as the id the daemon knows
cases.why: The translation itself, and the only case here that can see it. Every other case names a pane `p1` and gets `p1` on the wire, which is what makes them cases about the envelope - but above this file nothing spells a pane herdr's way, so what a request actually carries is the daemon's id for the name it was given. A registry that stopped translating would pass a Muster name through, herdr would not recognize it, and `pane.split` would split whatever it had focused and answer success.

cases.name: a pane name that resolves to nothing sends no request at all
cases.why: The reason resolution is a refusal rather than a pass-through. herdr ignores a `target_pane_id` it does not recognize and splits the pane it has focused instead, so a name for a pane that has closed - pasted out of an old log, or held by an agent that has been running since before it went - would silently split somebody else's work and report success. Refusing names the pane, which is what a person or an agent can act on.

expect.refused: no pane called p1w3r07bsd on local

cases.name: a split asking for a program sends no program
cases.why: herdr's pane.split takes no command and no label (`observations/herdr-0.8.0.md` section 18), so both have to happen once the pane exists. This is here because the failure of getting it wrong is silent in herdr's own particular way: a `command` or `label` key sent hopefully would be ignored without complaint, and the pane would come up nameless and running a bare shell - which looks exactly like a pane whose program exited immediately. What the pair actually adds up to is checked against a real daemon in `pane_equipping.rs`.

cases.name: text sent to a pane names the pane and carries no newline
cases.why: `pane_id` here rather than the `target_pane_id` a split takes, which is the same silent trap from the other side. And the text goes out exactly as given: Return is a second request, because herdr encodes a named key against the pane's live modes while a newline in this string is only a newline - and a program reading a bracketed paste treats those as different things, taking one as a submission and the other as more text to buffer.

cases.name: text sent without a Return is the same request
cases.why: Whether to press Return changes what happens after this request and nothing about this one, so the two spellings have to be identical here. A case that differed would mean the flag had leaked into the text - the failure being that a caller who asked for no Return got one, submitting a half-typed line to whatever is reading.

cases.name: a tab Muster named goes out as the id the daemon knows
cases.why: The tab half of the translation, and the only case here that can see it. Every other tab case names a tab `t1` and gets `t1` on the wire, which is what makes them cases about the envelope - but above this file nothing spells a tab herdr's way. A registry that stopped translating would pass a Muster name through, and herdr ignores a `tab_id` it does not recognize and renames whatever it has focused instead: somebody else's tab, relabelled, reported as success.

cases.name: a tab name that resolves to nothing sends no request at all
cases.why: The reason a tab resolves to a refusal rather than a pass-through, which is the same reason a pane does. The daemon holds one tab and the caller names a different one - a tab that has closed, read out of an older `muster window` or held by a script that has been running since it went. Passed through, herdr would ignore a `tab_id` it does not recognize and rename whichever tab it has focused, and answer success. Refusing names the tab, which is something a person or an agent can act on.

expect.refused: no tab called t1w3r0a4a9 on local
